newsitem.title: RWANDA: Little joy for Hutu refugees in Kabila's victory.
newsitem.headline: Little joy for Hutu refugees in Kabila's victory.

text.p: Victory for Zaire's rebels gave their country at the heart of Africa a new name and leader but brought little prospect of relief for hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees sheltering in the country.

As Laurent Kabila -- self-proclaimed president of the new Democratic Republic of Congo -- prepares for his triumphant arrival in the capital Kinshasa, tens of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees remain scattered through the country's forests.
Aid officials expect their problems only to multiply as Kabila's rebels tighten their grip on areas already under their control and extend into new pockets of territory in the east.
They however hope that for those who are located and want to go home, Kabila's alliance may cooperate more with repatriation.
But tens of thousands of those who have returned are locked up in Rwandan jails. Hundreds of thousands more returnees have resumed their subsistence existence under fear and suspicion.
Kabila spent more than 30 years as a rebel leader with little to show for it, but ironically, his sudden success since last year was largely connected to the Rwandans in eastern Zaire.
The refugees fled their homeland in 1994 to escape reprisal for the genocide of up to 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
More than two million Hutus settled in camps in eastern Zaire and Tanzania, among them tens of thousands of former Rwandan troops and Interahamwe militiamen who led the genocide.
From their bases in the camps, they stepped up punishing Hutu raids into Rwanda to the frustration of Kigali's rulers.

But in October last year, a deputy governor in the Zairean border city of Bukavu declared all Banyamulenge should be expelled into Rwanda following a series of clashes with local tribes and the Zairean army.
The Banyamulenge, ethnic Tutsis who settled in eastern Zaire up to 200 years ago and had close links to Kabila, had long been regarded with hostility by other Zaireans and the Rwandan Hutu refugees.

Kabila's rebellion initially drew strongly on Banyamulenge support and focused on clearing the Rwandan refugee camps, sending a hard core trekking further into Zaire and some 600,000 others back home.
More than 300,000 Rwandan Hutus plunged deeper into Africa's third largest country to escape the Tutsi-dominated rebels.
Some refugees including former troops and militia even managed to reach Congo on Zaire's western border after crossing on foot a country the size of western Europe.
But most remain trapped in the jungles and forests of east Zaire. Up to 100,000 were finally overcome by hunger, exhaustion and disease near Kisangani and pleaded to be allowed to go home.
Much of their readinesss to return evaporated last month when rebel forces attacked their camps and triggered a slaughter that aid officials believe may have resulted in thousands of deaths.

A huge area of rebel-held eastern Zaire has remained off-limits to aid workers since then but aid agencies need the cooperation of rebel authorities for an airlift which has so far repatriated more than 30,000 refugees from the Kisangani area.
Some Zaireans say rebels are carrying huge amounts of wood to a point 52 kms (28 miles) south of Kisangani to burn bodies of dead refugees and scatter the ashes in the Zaire river.
Aid workers dare not speak in public about what they fear for the refugees in case they further anger Kabila's officials and jeopardise chances of helping those they have reached.
But privately they say Kabila's swift advance on Kinshasa deflected international attention from the missing refugees.
Kigali, meanwhile, has denounced the refugees who refuse to head back and any new countries which may harbour them.

A senior aide to Rwandan Vice-President and Defence Minister Major-General Paul Kagame last week accused the Central African Republic bordering northwestern Zaire of harbouring those responsible for the genocide.
"We take strong exception to the Central African Republic which is taking in killers who have fled Zaire. They are taking them in without disarming them, a mistake Zaire made in 1994," he warned.
Aid officials fear that with Kabila consolidating his power across the country, he will find he has much less to fear from the international community over his treatment of the refugees.
